title: The Alarmist: Spinning and Wedging Out in Prelude and Fugue No.5, Book I
content_blocks: If J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier is the model for this entire set, then this prelude is the most traditional in texture. It features a moving, arpeggiating line in sixteenth-notes, against a slower line in quarter-notes. The arpeggiating lines develop into overlapping downward lines that cover the range of the piano, leading to a return of the original texture at different pitch levels. This process repeats until it returns to the opening one last time.

Where the prelude is relatively traditional in texture and gesture, the fugue is far from Bach in style.  The subject wedges out, getting alternatively higher and lower away from the starting point, and features rhythmic compression and decompression after the burst of seven repeated notes.  Since the mode for this pair of pieces (the same as No.11—see “The Pompous One,” August 31, 2025) restarts at the twelfth (just over one and a half octaves), stating the subject one or more octaves apart will result in a “diatonic answer” (see “Diatonic Answers: An Explainer,” July 3, 2025):  the same scale degree pattern transposed to start on a different scale degree, which can sound substantially different.  The first two sections of this four-voice fugue each end with a cadence.  An episode oscillates its way to the top of the keyboard, at which point downward arpeggios echo the prelude.  This leads to a final section in which the last statement, after wedging out, ends by wedging in to a closing E.

So why did I call this “The Alarmist” four years ago?  My best guess is that I was thinking about the burst of seven repeated notes at the start of the fugue subject.  Or perhaps it was the accelerations and decelerations in the fugue which can seem a bit histrionic, I suppose.  Anyway, that only applies to the fugue.  If anybody can suggest a name that applies both to the fugue and to the gloriously spinning out prelude, and I would appreciate knowing it.

Watching the videos of Steve playing this and other preludes and fugues, I am always amazed at his level of virtuosity. To focus on just one example, at about 0:37 into the Prelude, without looking where his right hand is going he moves his hand more than a foot and a half away, to land precisely on a key that is only about 7/8” wide. And he makes it look easy!

Where the prelude is relatively traditional in texture and gesture, the fugue is far from Bach in style.  The subject wedges out, getting alternatively higher and lower away from the starting point, and features rhythmic compression and decompression after the burst of seven repeated notes.
